findings.label: Cherry-red spot on fundus photography
findings.evidence: Colour retinography showing a classic macular cherry-red spot (Patient VII)

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Slit-lamp photograph of the lens showing cortical and nuclear dot-like opacities in Patient VI with sialidosis type I; lens opacities are a described manifestation (100% of cohort) but are not in the allowed vocabulary, so they are recorded as proposed findings. B: Colour fundus photography of Patient VII showing a textbook classic macular cherry-red spot, the hallmark retinal manifestation of sialidosis type I. C: Colour fundus photographs of Patients IV and VIII showing faded macular cherry-red spots with reduced foveal contrast; a recognized less striking variant of the classic cherry-red spot in sialidosis type I. D: Infrared retinography and fundus autofluorescence of Patient I demonstrating the macular cherry-red spot region; multimodal imaging of the same sialidosis type I retinal manifestation described in the article.

panels.figure_caption: Ophthalmological features of patients with sialidosis type I. (A) Cortical and nuclear dot-like lens opacities (Patient VI). (B) Colour retinography showing a classic macular cherry-red spot (Patient VII). (C) Colour retinography showing a faded macular cherry-red spot in Patients IV (left) and VIII (right). (D) Multimodal imaging showing an infrared retinography on the left and autofluorescence imaging on the right (both from Patient I).
in_text_mentions: The corneas of our patients were clear. All of them (100%) presented visually non-significant changes on their lenses (figure 1A), such as scattered white speckles and punctate opacities affecting the cortex or the nucleus.

All patients presented with a macular cherry-red spot (figure 1B). African American patients presented with a darker ‘cherry-brown’ spot due to the increased pigment density in their RPE. Qualitatively, the patient with the least clear macular cherry-red spot by colour fundus imaging was Patient IV, followed by Patient VIII (figure 1C). This difficulty was due to a faded pale ring surrounding the obscured fovea, causing a less striking contrast between the foveal spot and the retina.
